Moving a discussion that I started in private to here. I asked Mario about the state of the level algorithms in lean4lean and learned that

  • https://github.com/digama0/lean4lean/blob/master/Lean4Lean/Level.lean should be complete, but has a bug
  • it also has normalization, but that’s not complete
  • the thesis describes something simpler (where you just case split on any imax's after normalization gets stuck), and it’s not clear which one is better™
  • neither provides a true normalization
  • normalization may only be relevant for good cache hits, not functionally

I think that actually answers all my questions, so no more discussion to move here, but thanks for the insights, @Mario Carneiro :-)

I still hope we can fix the new algorithm. If we extend the level grammar, then it is a normalization in that extended grammar of so-called "sublevels", and if we use the second part of the algorithm to bring it back to levels, then it should be a real normalization. I just keep trying to avoid doing things that are exponential and possibly that's required
I take it from #lean4lean > State of the Proof @ 💬 that the previous night was really productive and that the level algorithm is now complete? Are any of the prior points still an issue?
that is correct. The third point is still true

I also added an optimization to the algorithm to avoid booting up the expensive stuff when simple lean-style rewrites are good enough to do the normalization. It's about 30x faster to do what lean does, and that works in the 99.8% of level expressions that don't have imax after simple rewriting
After some discussion with @Yoan Géran , I learned (and proved) an interesting fact: Level equivalence and inequality testing in the imax algebra is coNP-complete
which kind of addresses point 3 above... any algorithm here is going to have to do either a DNF style expansion or a DPLL-style case tree. Or you can get fancy and use a sat solver

Rocq's theory is simpler, isn't it? Would there be an advantage of adopting it?
https://popl26.sigplan.org/details/rocqpl-2026-papers/11/Enhancing-universe-polymorphism-for-Rocq-Algebraic-universes-consistency-checking-a
yes, imax causes the problem, it's polynomial without it

Although Mathieu worked super hard to make the new, polynomial algorithm based on Bezem and Coquand's work as efficient as the old algorithm, which is exponential in theory but works well in practice, afaiu the new implementation is still not quite as fast as the old one. (Although this is complicated by the two kinds of universes (global vs polymorphic) and the need to handle cumulativity, so it's hard to have a proper apples-to-apples comparison here. and draw conclusions based on that for Lean)
It would be nice to get an apples-to-apples comparison to a sort polymorphic algebra with split kind and level a la rocq adapted to lean's universes
the part I'm not sure about is whether non-cumulativity causes problems. I'm currently looking into the unification problem, which is quite a bit more complicated

I have been looking into E-unification in the level algebra, and while it's easy to construct nonunique mgu's, e.g. max(?a,u)=umax(?a,u)=umax(?a,u)=u is solved by 000 and uuu, I had been hoping that there are at least finitely many solutions. It turns out, this is not the case: (cc @Yoan Géran )

Theorem. Mario Carneiro said:

yes, imax causes the problem, it's polynomial without it

I'm probably missing something obvious, but why not have 2 foralls? One for Prop and one for Type. Lean already has a lint for inductives that are needlessly polymorphic (if I'm not mistaken). What would be the consequences? Is Prop/Type polymorphism on forall a critical feature?
Polymorphism is never critical in theory, but in practice giving up on it means code duplication, which never nice, and not intellectually satisfying.

In theory, duplication is only necessary in the kernel, surface may avoid duplication. But I agree it's not nice. And whether it's intellectually satisfying is more complex, because in some sense those foralls are fundamentally different: one is relevant to computation, the other not. It's not obvious they can be described uniformly without losing something.

Another advantage (besides syntax directed interpretation rather than type directed) of distinguishing Prop and Type terms syntactically is that it simplifies checking whether something is a Prop (like to enforce elimination restrictions) which would have most probably avoided #14807. But I agree there's a non obvious trade-off between "soundness" (how simple is the metatheory), "expressivity" (how simple it is to derive a particular judgment), and "elegance" (how satisfying the design is)

That's true. It also makes the proof of a checker substantially easier. You can generate a Prop-motive small eliminator unconditionally and a Type u-motive large eliminator optionally, rather than Prop-motive vs an awkward Sort u unified eliminator, and these two have different numbers of universe arguments. For a proof as substantial as verifying a kernel, any cost savings are worth grabbing, otherwise you will be threading 100s of hypotheses of garbage everywhere :)

I don't think that's true. You don't need to have syntactically different objects for Prop and Type to determine whether it's the Prop or Type instance, this info can be recovered in constant time I think.
But in any case, surface syntax and internal syntax don't need to coincide, so it could still be internally like you say, while keeping the same surface syntax and just elaborate it away.

Yes exactly, having 2 separate languages (surface and kernel) with different priorities (usability and metatheory) and a sufficiently simple translation from surface to kernel (so we still understand the semantics of surface code), seems like it could disentangle some design questions
